text:
The Aiguille is a small formation, not a peak of its own: it is the cockscomb dividing the high Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on its west side and an unnamed glacier on its east, sitting just south of the Torment-Forbidden traverse line. It is named for its resemblance to the Chamonix aiguille of the same shape — a deliberate echo, and a coincidence worth being clear about rather than a mistake.

Approach exactly as for Forbidden Peak: Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles to the small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg, the old Diamond Mine roadbed, then the steep unmaintained climbers' path with several stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the Boston Basin camps at about 5,300 and 6,400 ft.

From camp, head up toward the Forbidden Gully / Cat Scratch gullies area and traverse to the notch. It is a half-day objective from camp, which is most of its appeal.
runs: is the cockscomb dividing the high forbidden basin from torment basin with the taboo glacier on

text:
The formation is the easy part: the aiguille is conspicuous on entering Boston Basin and reads as the letter it is named for. Use it to orient the whole basin. The route is the harder part.

The base is the notch to the right of the north ridge — you traverse to it from the Cat Scratch / Forbidden Gully side; you do not start at the toe of the ridge. A start at the very bottom of the crest is not this route.

Count the pitches, because the count is the route: three to four pitches of fourth-class scrambling to the base of a tower, and then one 40-ft pitch to its top. That is the whole climb. If you have run out four pitches and there is no tower standing in front of you, you are on the wrong side of the formation.

The most important thing to know about the top is that it is not the top. The route finishes on a subsidiary tower; the true high point of the Aiguille looks as though it is about to topple over and most parties deliberately stop short of it. So a summit that feels wrong is not evidence you are off route — on this formation it is the expected outcome, and it is the reason the descent is a single 40-ft rappel from where you stand.

Tell it from the south ridge by which side you walked round. The two routes differ only in which flank of the same small formation is climbed from the same camp; the South Ridge is the longer, harder and much less documented of the two, and its start is not published — so if you are unsure which side you are on, the four-pitch scramble to a tower is the one that can be confirmed.
runs: the notch to the right of the north ridge

text: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin below Cutthroat Peak. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. On this approach the lake is on the way: the trail continues past it and climbs to Cutthroat Pass, from where the crest leads south about a mile to the base of the North Ridge. From the Rainy Pass side it is off the route entirely.
runs: mile to the base of the north ridge

text: From Tiffany Springs Campground (6,760 ft), hike trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (7,150 ft, ~45 minutes). From the pass, either traverse south on the grassy east slope to the small cirque at the base of the North Face (7,360 ft) and climb the boulder field to the base of the climb (7,600 ft), or hike the trail on the north side of the ridge toward Little Tiffany Lake and drop down to the base from above (~30 minutes). Three driving approaches reach the Tiffany Springs trailhead: via Conconully/North Fork Salmon Creek and FR 39 (~21 mi, ~1 hr, rough road, 4WD recommended); via the South Fork/Baldy Pass (~30.6 mi, ~2 hr, 2WD-passable gravel); or via the Methow Valley (~26.5 mi, ~1 hr, 2WD gravel). An alternate trailhead at Freezeout Pass (via East Chewuch Rd/FR 37/FR 39 from Winthrop) also accesses the area and does not require a Northwest Forest Pass.
runs: pass either traverse south on the grassy east slope to the small cirque at the base of the
and climb the boulder field to the base of the climb
the trail on the north side of the ridge
little tiffany lake and drop down to the base

text:
Tiffany Springs Campground sits at about 6,760 ft and is reached by long gravel drives from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek road, from the Methow Valley, or over Baldy Pass on the South Fork. The Conconully line is the roughest of the three. Expect an hour or more on gravel whichever you choose.

Trail #373 leaves the campground east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft, about forty-five minutes of easy walking. From the pass, traverse south on the grassy east slope below the crest into the small cirque at the base of the north face, at roughly 7,360 ft, then climb the boulder field to the foot of the climbing at about 7,600 ft.

Compared with anything else in this corner of the state the approach is short and easy, which is most of this face's appeal. Roads are snowbound for much of the year and generally open around late June.
runs: the small cirque at the base of the

text: Pitch 3 counterintuitively downclimbs about 15 ft off the crest before working up and right on ramps to a vertical seam and cutting back left to a ledge (5.7) — don't be thrown off by losing height here.
runs: up and right on ramps to a vertical seam

text: From the lowest point of the buttress (Kearney start), gain the rock and head for wide, broken cracks.
runs: gain the rock and head for wide broken cracks

text: Get into the main dihedral and pull a series of tougher moves, including a shallow, somewhat dirty chimney; the Kearney and Beckey start variations converge above here.
runs: get into the main dihedral and pull a series of tougher moves including a shallow

text: The lower section, most commonly climbed by the left-hand start, takes wide broken cracks on solid rock to gain the crest below a large headwall. Above that, downclimb about 15 ft off the crest and work up and right on ramps to a vertical seam, then back left to a ledge at around 5.7. The pitch into the main dihedral includes a shallow chimney at 5.7 to 5.8 and is the dirtiest part of the route — moss, loose gravel and old fixed pins marking the way. Two established starts exist and mixing them up is the usual route-finding error.
runs: work up and right on ramps to a vertical seam then back left to a ledge

text: A deep objective reached along the same corridor as its neighbours, and the walk-in is a full day or more of committing glaciated terrain rather than a hike. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, take the maintained trail to the pass, then leave it and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow bands, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake, climb out of the basin toward the cliff band running west off the knoll above; the Red Ledge cuts through it, usually entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin and a few feet of easy rock, and it is broad and walkable unless it is holding snow or verglas. Roughly a quarter mile past the ledge, descend several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between the two large icefall sections, cross that bench, and continue to the foot of the Formidable Glacier. Note that this is a different objective from the peak's ordinary walk-up on the south side, which is the descent line rather than the approach.
runs: bench and continue to the foot of the formidable glacier

text: small-medium alpine rock rack to 3 inches
runs: small medium alpine rock rack to 3 inches

text: Grade: 5.7+ YDS, Grade IV, 12 pitches, 4,000 feet. First ascent: 1963. Route: Climb partway up C-J couloir to hanging glacier on right; ascend leftmost rib to summit. Hazards: Objective danger from falling rock/ice, steep snow, exposed scrambling, avalanche potential. Equipment: Small-to-medium alpine rock rack (to 3 inches), 10+ runners, helmet. Best season: July-September. No bush climbing.
runs: medium alpine rock rack to 3 inches 10+ runners helmet

text: Very low — an estimated 3–5 ascents per year by any route on the NE face as a whole (not this line specifically)
runs: 3 5 ascents per year by any route

text: Straight off the road end: the C-J couloir to the hanging glacier, then the leftmost rib
runs: the c j couloir to the hanging glacier

text:
This is one of the shortest approaches in the range and one of the least forgiving. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road near 3,600 ft, walk a short way back down the road, descend a dirt embankment, ford or cross the infant Cascade River, and cross the terminal moraine and snowfield. Serious ground starts around 3,500 ft — you are on the route within an hour of the car.

Climb partway up the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir to the hanging glacier on the right, then take the leftmost rib to the summit. Twelve pitches, about 4,000 ft.

The descent is a separate expedition: the East Ridge's loose 3rd and 4th class gendarme ledges to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, then either the couloir or 'Doug's Direct' — beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehilling steep heather, across Mixup Peak's north ridge and down to the Cache Glacier. Parties have taken four and a half to nine hours from the col.
runs: couloir to the hanging glacier on the right

text: From the north basin below the peak, climb a snow finger (loose/dirty rock in late season) to a notch at the base of the northwest arete, then follow straightforward route-finding up blocky, generally solid Class 4 to 5.6 rock; a standout pitch 5 climbs a steep corner on good holds, with a choice of corner systems higher up (the right-hand option is easier). Black lichen on the granite becomes extremely slick when wet.
runs: a notch at the base of the northwest arete

text: Ascend a right-facing corner to reach easy ground and a good stance at the base of a steeper face.
runs: stance at the base of a steeper face

text: Do not rappel the fall line from station 1. Traverse skier's left (north) and down a short, loose gully. A rappel is possible here and many parties simply downclimb it - which is why counts of three and four both appear for this descent.
runs: traverse skier's left north and down a short loose gully

text: The final station drops to the slopes near the Argonaut-Colchuck col, where the technical descent ends and the walk to Colchuck Lake begins.
runs: to the slopes near the argonaut colchuck col

text:
From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail and go straight past the Colchuck Lake turnoff. Continue to about 4,700 ft, where a faint path leaves the trail for Mountaineer Creek. Follow it over and down to the creek, then up the creek to roughly 4,780 ft, and bushwhack up to a boulder field below Argonaut at about 4,925 ft.

Traverse the boulders following cairns south-southwest and cut through slide alder — this brush is the notorious part of the day, and staying on talus to climber's right where you can avoids the worst of it. Then head up in or beside the trees, through boulders, talus, scree and dry creek beds, past waterfall slabs, into the north basin below Argonaut at about 6,700 ft. Roughly four hours car-to-basin for an efficient party.

Expect to lose the boot path in the boulder field. Most of this approach is navigated by feel; there is no marked trail. Wet, mossy logs over Mountaineer Creek are a nuisance in both directions.
runs: then up the creek to roughly 4 780
up to a boulder field below argonaut at

text: Leave the trail at the bridge and travel cross-country south into the mouth of Summit Chief Valley, then up the valley to the flat gravel wash at about 4,650 ft.
runs: the flat gravel wash at about 4 650

text: P1 is a committing traverse and corner (~10 hard moves) to a ledge belay; P2 is a right-facing corner with limited feet and hard gear placement (5.11a); P3 is a chimney then vegetated crack over a block (~5.8); P4 is a scramble approach to the overhangs; P5 pulls a pair of obvious overhangs with good protection (~5.10); P6 finishes with hand-crack climbing to the summit (~5.9).
runs: right facing corner with limited feet and hard gear placement

text: The Blue Lake Trailhead is on the south side of SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) a little under a mile west of Washington Pass, between mileposts 161 and 162, about 42 miles east of Newhalem or 31 miles west of Winthrop. The paved lot is small and fills early. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required.
runs: trailhead is on the south side of sr 20

text: This ridge was first climbed in 2018 as one leg of the 'Boston Marathon' — a ~26.2-mile, mostly-soloed technical traverse circling the entire rim of Boston Basin (26 pitches up to 5.8 R, 26 rappels, 20,000+ ft of technical terrain). The ridge itself is deep, virgin choss rated 5.5 X, including a two-pitch section climbed à cheval (straddling the ridge crest) across rock with the consistency of feta cheese, followed by roughly 1,000 additional feet of similarly poor climbing. It is accessed along the basin rim from the direction of Sharkfin Tower. There is no established description of this specific ridge as an independent route — treat it as an obscure, rarely-repeated line rather than a maintained trade route.
runs: 26 pitches up to 5.8 r 26 rappels

text: Gap on the southeast side of Sharkfin Tower where Boston's northwest ridge begins. The loose gully above the bergschrund below the tower leads up to it; the only known ascent instead came over Sharkfin Tower and traversed a steep hanging snow slope to the base of the ridge.
runs: sharkfin tower and traversed a steep hanging snow slope

text: The only documented ascent gained this ridge after climbing Sharkfin Tower, descending from it, and traversing a steep hanging snow slope directly to the base of the ridge. There is no established independent approach to the foot of the crest, so the snow condition on that traverse is the gatekeeper and it is committing terrain to cross in poor conditions.
runs: a steep hanging snow slope directly to the base of the

text: The variation rejoins the standard NW Face route above pitch 3 (it climbs a more direct crack to the same belay ledge the original pitch 3 reaches), so pitches 4-5 and the descent are identical to the Northwest Face: from the west summit, scramble to the top of the Beckey Route and use its rappel line. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail.
runs: downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem

text: The most direct of the three summit-block finishes: a single ~80-ft pitch straight up the north face on mostly solid rock. It's the cleanest line on the pinnacle and conveniently shares ground with the north-side rappel descent.
runs: up the north face on mostly solid rock

text: From the snow at the north side of the summit block, climb straight up the north face on mostly solid rock; the few 5.3-5.4 moves come low, then it eases. Protect with three or four small-to-medium cams and a few nuts, and belay the party up from the slung boulder on top. Late season a moat at the base can add climbing or force a committing step onto the rock.
runs: up the north face on mostly solid rock

text: A deep, sometimes near-impassable snow moat opens on the east side of the Middle Peak by mid/late season — parties have had to improvise crossings (e.g. wedged ice blocks) when the snow bridge is gone
runs: on the east side of the middle peak

text: A quirky single pitch beginning on blocky, scrambly ground at the downhill end of the Ice Box, climbing deceptively low-angle dark rock past an exposed traverse to an arete, then a bolted leftward traverse near the top to an anchor shared with a neighboring unnamed trad line.
runs: at the downhill end of the ice box

text: Begins on blocky terrain at the downhill (toward-the-hairpin) end of the wall. Above the scrambly start the rock looks deceptively low-angle; scramble the lower section and trend right as it steepens, aiming for the arete after a short, exposed rightward traverse. Continue up varied knobs, crimps, and jugs. Near the top, traverse left on bolts through steeper, similarly-featured climbing to the anchors — the position and quality of climbing are better than the route looks from the ground, though the bolts themselves can be hard to spot before starting.
runs: steepens aiming for the arete after a short exposed rightward traverse continue

text: Follows a left-facing, broken corner system with sustained, quality climbing and comfortable belay stations. Watch for loose rock on P2 near the treed ledge, including stacked blocks at the top of the corner that should be treated with care.
runs: stacked blocks at the top of the corner

text: Doubles from BD 0.1 to 3; a #4 is handy but not required. A rack of nuts, and RP-style micro-nuts, are nice to have for thin placements.
runs: to 3 a 4 is handy but not required

text: Climb up and left onto the treed ledge, watching for loose rock, then enter the left-slanting crack and tight, flaring corner. Gear is small (0.1-size cams and RPs) and fiddly. Do not pull on the chockstone and stacked blocks at the top. A 5.10 bypass goes straight up the narrowing crack before cutting left up a hidden ramp to rejoin the corner. Belay at a tree on the ledge above.
runs: left up a hidden ramp to rejoin the corner

text: Climb a short, bushy wide hand crack to a treed ledge, then continue up the featured face and broken crack-and-corner system toward the clean left-facing dihedral above. Step right just before the dihedral to belay on a mossy ledge. With enough gear, pitches 2 and 3 are often linked.
runs: left facing dihedral above step right just before the dihedral

text: Loose rock on the second pitch, including stacked blocks at the top of the corner
runs: stacked blocks at the top of the corner

text:
Do not stop at the obvious base. The first thing you reach under this wall is a granite patio where two other routes start about fifty feet apart. This route is not there. It is about a hundred and fifty feet climbers' left of and above that patio, so from the patio you keep walking left and gaining height rather than racking up.

The marker is vegetation, and it is specific: a small outcropping of trees uphill of the left-hand patio route's start. Find that patch of trees. The route begins in the rock-scarred open book just left of it. Scarred rock and an open book, immediately left of a small stand of trees, uphill and left of the patio — that is the whole identification, and it is the only start on this wall with a plant landmark.

Confirm by the feature above: this line takes the obvious left-facing broken corner system in the centre of the buttress, left of the blockier ground that carries the two patio routes. If the corner above you faces right rather than left, you are on the wrong side of the wall.

Negative markers. If you are standing on a flat slab platform with a second route start visible fifty feet away, you are still at the patio and have not walked far enough. If your line is wandering through featured ground past big gnarled trees and later a distinctly spiral tree, you are on the 5.9 that starts right of the patio.

This route is also the one on the wall whose descent is different, and knowing that is worth a lot at the top: parties find it faster to rappel the route — three full sixty-metre rappels reach the ground, starting from a tree slightly up and left of the belay at the top of pitch five — rather than take the shared notch descent. Watch for stacked blocks near the top of the second pitch's corner.
runs: a small outcropping of trees uphill of the
the obvious left facing broken corner system in the
reach the ground starting from a tree slightly up and left

text: Starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the base of the Classic Route; climbs up and left toward the shared anchors (block with tat and rings) used by The Roof.
runs: at two wide left leaning cracks about 50
right of the base of the classic route

text: South slope to the south side of the summit block, right of the Classic Route
runs: to the south side of the summit block

text: Identical trailhead-to-basin approach as the Classic Route and The Roof: from the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, hike the maintained Snow Lake Trail ~1 mile (about 350 ft of up-and-down) to Snow Lake, the last water source. Continue past the lake on the fading tread over a wooded rise, then pick a line up and right into the talus/dirt gully on the peak's NW side; a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the gully's top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to the saddle (Unicorn Col) just west/southwest of the summit, then follow the use trail traversing below the cliffs on the south side of the peak to the base of the summit horn. The Open Book line starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the Classic Route on the same south face, so from the base of the horn move climber's-right before starting the technical climbing; it's regarded as the easiest of the summit-block lines (Easy 5th class / 5.0), a step down from the Classic Route (5.4-5.6) and The Roof (5.6). Total approach is roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.
runs: at two wide left leaning cracks about 50

text:
Leave the trail at the stream crossing just before the lake, not at the lake. Two independent accounts do exactly that: cross the stream, head north-east up into open forest, and break out of the trees onto talus.

The arrival test is the ground itself. The talus is continuous and endless — no benches, no trees, no interruption — running roughly fourteen hundred feet straight to the top. There is no elegant line on it; you put your head down and climb. If you are still weaving between trees and heather benches you have not reached the slope proper.

Negative marker for leaving too early: one climber went up toward what he took to be the south-west ridge, found it was not, and had to work up and down to reach the real one, where bits of use trail run through the least-bad talus. Use-trail fragments are a sign you are on the right slope.

Summit test: the top is ringed by cliffs on every side except the scree slope you came up. If you are on a summit with more than one walkable side, it is not this one.

How to know it is Osceola and not Carru: Mount Carru is about a mile east and it is higher — 8,595 ft against Osceola's 8,587. From the top of Osceola you look east across a deep notch at a higher peak. The ground between the two is described by one climber as somewhere between awful and impassable, so that notch is a wall, not a link. Osceola, Carru and Lago all keep their steep and cliffy ground on the north, which gives a broader check: a peak in this group whose easy ground is on the north side is none of the three.

Nothing published reports a false summit on Osceola.
runs: at the stream crossing just before the lake

text:
From the Icicle Road junction at the west end of Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Walk the Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill for roughly two to two and a half miles — about an hour — until the wall stands directly opposite you across the drainage. The trail never touches the rock, so what you are watching for is the wall coming abeam, not a junction or a sign.

At one of the first easy openings, branch right off the trail and scramble down into the flat ground beside Snow Creek to find the log crossing. On the far bank, climb up through boulders and talus until a bootpath forms; it gains about 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall.

Weekends are busy and this is the most popular route in Leavenworth — a queue at the base is normal.
runs: 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall

text:
Find the route by its top, not its bottom. Outer Space is the long, well-cleaned crack splitting the upper headwall — the Shield — and it is the most obvious single feature on the wall. Trace that crack downward to where it ends at a ledge with several bushes on it.

The route's own original start is the ledge-and-dihedral system about 80 ft right of that point and 100 ft down from it.

In practice most parties never use that start: they climb the first pitches of Remorse instead, which begins essentially where the climbers' trail arrives at the wall. That arrival point is the highest part of the wall's base, with a few small scrub trees on it. Standing there, the clean bolted slab straight in front of you is RPM's first pitch at 5.10d; Remorse's much easier line is the often-vegetated gully about 30 ft to the right of it.

So the single most useful test at the base: if your first move off the ground is a hard, blank, bolted friction slab, you are on RPM, not on the Remorse start to Outer Space. Step right into the scruffy gully.
runs: the long well cleaned crack splitting the upper headwall

text: From I-90 exit 34 go north, then right onto SE Middle Fork Road, FR 56, and follow it about twelve miles to the Taylor River junction. Bear right onto FR 5620 and continue to the Dingford Creek trailhead at roughly 1,500 ft. FR 56 is notorious for potholes and ruts and high clearance is genuinely useful; the stretch beyond the gate is reported to be in better shape than the public road. FR 5620 is decommissioned beyond Dingford Creek. The closed stretch to the old Dutch Miller Gap trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp is given as seven, eight or ten miles, so do not plan on a precise number. A bike is universally recommended and cuts hours off both ends. Beyond the road, parties use three genuinely different lines, none of them confirmed by another, so read all three before choosing. The most specific of them fords the Middle Fork on a visual cue rather than a mileage: walk roughly four miles of trail until you can see the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the foot of Overcoat. Push through about ten minutes of alder, ford there, and you land on the talus field at the base of those cliffs. Further north-east the alder gets much thicker. A second line crosses about a mile before the Dutch Miller Gap trail proper and climbs steep forest to camp at Overcoat Lake. A third crosses the river on rocks, climbs steep brushy ground into a two-mile rocky corridor sometimes called the Valley of the Chiefs, meets continuous snow around 4,600 ft, and goes over a pass at about 6,140 ft. On the traverse toward camp, one party's correction: they climbed to the ridge and then realised the line stays lower, and had to drop back to find the sloping rock crux and downclimb to the snow. A durable warning about the road rather than the mountain: the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road has a long-standing reputation for unsavoury activity, including gunfire, and at least one regular visitor reports it on every trip.
runs: see the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the

text:
The snow finger is not visible until you are underneath it, so do not try to identify it from camp or from the glacier below.

The sequence that works: reach the Overcoat Glacier, make a long rising traverse of five hundred feet or so to the top of the mild glacier, and only then does the steep snow finger show itself, with dark towers standing above it.

The dark towers are the transition. You leave snow for rock at their foot, then round the corner east and the glacier reappears below you. From there it is steep gully climbing on solid holds with a few exposed steps over tall blocks to the summit.

The consistent fact across every published account, and the one to steer by: the summit pyramid is gained on its east or north-east side. Nobody describes climbing it from the south-east. If you are working around to the south side of the block looking for a way up, you have gone the wrong way round.

Grade opinions on that finish run from Class 3 to low fifth, and parties have pitched it out in two short pitches with a few small cams and nuts, with one rappel and some downclimbing to get back to the top of the snow finger. Expect thin protection and poor rock rather than a scramble.

Moats around the glacier margin and crevasses part way up the snow finger are the two things that most often force a detour here, and both were reported as more awkward than expected by parties who had read otherwise.
runs: to get back to the top of the

text: The final block stands roughly 400 vertical ft above the surrounding terrain and is steep on every side, so at least class 4 and arguably low 5th is unavoidable to reach the top. Climb the steep gully on the east side of the pyramid on generally good holds with a few exposed moves over tall steps to gain a roomy summit. Summit rocks have been described as wobbly — test everything, and be aware that anyone below is directly in the fall line. Descent is normally a downclimb through a dihedral and heather ledges followed by two full-length rappels back to the glacier, so bring enough rope and slings to build anchors.
runs: a few exposed moves over tall steps to

text: Pernod and neighboring Chablis are the easiest of the Wine Spires, and this line is a reasonable day from a Burgundy Col camp. The climbing is moderate (about 5.5-5.7) and not sustained. It climbs from the east side up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti and then up the northeast corner to a tiny summit block; the South Face and the Direct West Face are separate, harder routes on the same spire.
runs: are the easiest of the wine spires and

text:
This line is climbed from the east, not from the west face gully. Stay on the main climbers' trail past the bench all the way to Burgundy Col; the gully that contours right off the bench leads to the base of the west face, which is the start of a different and much harder route.

From the col, cross to the east side and go south. Traverse below the east walls of Chianti and then Pernod, on snow and talus at the edge of the glacier basin. Pernod is the highest of the four spires and sits just south of Chianti.

The key feature is the notch between Chianti and Pernod. From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to that notch; the ground is mostly 4th and 5th class, roughly three pitches. Going south from the col you pass below Chianti first, and the notch you want is the one immediately south of it. The next notch beyond Pernod separates Pernod from Chablis and is the wrong one.

From the notch the route goes up the northeast corner to the small summit block, which carries old first-ascent bolts that are worth backing up.

For parties who camp high: Burgundy Col holds three or four bivy sites, one large enough for a two-person tent, with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing. Those shelters are a positive identification of the col.

Descent is by rappel: back to the notch, then long rappels down the east side to the snow at the edge of the glacier basin. From there climb back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' trail.
runs: leads to the base of the west face

text: The standard approach to Phantom Peak uses the Southwest Glacier and South Couloir with a snow ramp at approximately 40-45 degrees. Climbers cross a bergschrund, navigate a steep snow finger, then move onto broken rock with Class 2-3 scrambling before traversing the sharp, exposed summit ridge. The summit consists of solid granitic rock with thrilling exposure on both sides. A hand line or belay may be useful for the narrowest sections.
runs: of solid granitic rock with thrilling exposure on both sides

text: From a roping-up ledge just above the 6,100' saddle in the ridge's lower reaches, pitch 1 starts with a short, steep crack system before rambling along the crest. Pitches 2-5 continue in the same vein — large corners, towers either bypassed or climbed directly, and exposed ridge running, mostly 5.7+. Pitch 6 holds the crux: a tough move over an airy four-foot-wide cleft, requiring a long 5.10-ish stemming move across a 100-ft-deep gap (the FA party rigged a nut-and-sling handhold to tension across, then top-roped it free). At the top of pitch 7 the ridge tops out on a tower, from which the party rappelled ~100 ft into a notch; pitches 8-10 offer aesthetic face and crack climbing on solid rock. As the difficulty eases, the rope is coiled and about 400 ft of 4th-class terrain is soloed to the sharp summit ridge, finishing with an exposed traverse to the final summit pinnacle.
runs: 6 100 saddle in the ridge's lower reaches

text: An involved two-day approach: ~10 miles on trail up and over Hannegan Pass, wading the Chilliwack River, traversing the scenic 5-mile Easy Ridge, soloing exposed 4th-class terrain across the 'Imperfect Impasse,' climbing through Perfect Pass and over the Challenger Glacier, then descending and traversing steep snow, talus, and more glacier to a bivy site under Ghost Peak (Phantom Peak's neighbor immediately to the north), from which the full west ridge comes into view.
runs: miles on trail up and over hannegan pass
through perfect pass and over the challenger glacier then

text: From the summit, downclimb the southeast face, including a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall (the FA party noted this crossing would be more straightforward earlier in the season, with more snow cover), circling back to the bivy camp under Ghost Peak.
runs: a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall

text:
An involved two-day approach. Roughly 10 miles on trail up and over Hannegan Pass, wading the Chilliwack River, then the scenic 5-mile traverse of Easy Ridge, soloing exposed 4th-class terrain across the Imperfect Impasse, climbing through Perfect Pass and over the Challenger Glacier, then descending and traversing steep snow, talus and more glacier to a bivy site.

The route was first climbed in July 2021 and is documented in a single first-ascent account, so treat everything about it as sparsely reported.
runs: miles on trail up and over hannegan pass

text:
The bivy is the viewpoint and that is the point of it: the camp sits under Ghost Peak, Phantom's neighbour immediately to the north, and the first-ascent party chose it because the full west ridge comes into view from there. So the test is not a feature at the base of the climb but a named peak overhead: if the summit above your camp is not Ghost Peak, and Phantom is not the next summit south of you, you are camped in the wrong place.

Why that matters more than usual here: this ridge has one published ascent. Nobody has recorded a marker at its toe, and inventing one would be inventing the only fact that matters. What is recorded is the vantage point, so use it: from camp, with the ridge in view, pick the line and note it before the cloud comes in. This is a route to reconnoitre the evening before rather than to find in the morning.

What going too far looks like, on the approach: past Perfect Pass, the Challenger Glacier is crossed and then left again on the far side. If you are still gaining height on ice you have not started the descent toward the Ghost Peak bivy.

On the descent, and worth knowing before you start: the way off is the southeast face, including a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall. The first-ascent party noted that crossing would be more straightforward earlier in the season with more snow cover.
runs: a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall

text: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
runs: to the western slope of the range from

text: Stevens Canyon Road — the only access to the Reflection Lakes trailhead — is gated and closed each winter, typically reopening in stages from late May into June and closing again by late October or November depending on snowpack; check the NPS road status page before driving out. The route also skirts the Butter Creek Research Natural Area, which is closed to public entry without a research permit.
runs: the butter creek research natural area which is closed to public

text: From the top, traverse the summit ridge of the Blob northward toward the Blob/Terror col — an adventure in its own right, with short simul-climbing recommended over the exposed crest. At the col edge, locate webbing rappel anchors over a steep step and make two rappels down into the notch. From the notch, an easy scramble down the col returns climbers to the bench below.

text: The Silver Horn is a sub-summit on the east ridge of Silver Star Mountain, east of the main summit, and both of its routes are on the clean white granite of its south face. That face is not reached from the Wine Spires pullout or Burgundy Col, which serve the other side of the crest. Instead, walk the Cedar Creek Trail from its trailhead at the end of FR 5310-200, off SR-20 about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turnoff. After roughly five miles, turn off to the right below the old burn and follow a rough path up the right-hand side of the creek that drains the south side of the Silver Horn. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping below the face.
runs: drains the south side of the silver horn

text: From the Longmire Wilderness Information Center (2,762 ft), pick up the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles in, after climbing out of Longmire, the trail drops steeply (~400+ ft) to a log-bridge crossing of Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically damaged or washed out by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier, so check current status at the Longmire WIC before you leave, since a failed crossing can force a long reroute. Beyond the creek the trail climbs by switchbacks through old-growth forest, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek, and traverses a ridge past Devil's Dream backcountry camp (~5 mi, reliable water) before breaking out of the trees into the subalpine meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 mi and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin and open views of the Tahoma/South Tahoma icefall. From Indian Henry's, leave the maintained Wonderland Trail and follow the Mirror Lakes spur/climbers' path (several plank crossings over marshy meadow, then end of maintained tread), continuing cross-country onto the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak between about 6,000 and 6,300 ft to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. Running water is often available here from snowmelt puddles into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at ~6,300 ft (with running water nearby) is another common first-night camp for a 2-day ascent. From Point 6631, drop briefly NNE to a saddle at about 6,400 ft — the start of Success Cleaver proper. Many parties place a second high camp on the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft (snow platforms can be dug in), from which the route continues up the crest — including a knife-edge section that requires real scrambling once snow melts off it — before angling climber's-right up snow gullies that merge onto the Kautz Cleaver around 12,200–12,600 ft, then up steepening snow/ice (to roughly 45°, with an isolated ~15 ft step near 55° used to bypass a cliff band in some seasons) to Point Success at 14,158 ft. All-in this is roughly 12–13 miles and 11,500 ft of gain from Longmire to Point Success, so most parties split it over 2 days with an intermediate camp rather than going car-to-car in a single push.
runs: the southwest and west slopes of pyramid peak between

text:
Longmire (2,762 ft) is the start, on the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles out the trail drops steeply to cross Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically wrecked by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier. Ask at the Longmire wilderness desk before you leave, because a failed crossing means a long reroute rather than a wet foot.

Beyond Kautz Creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp (about 5 miles, reliable water) before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 miles and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin.

At Indian Henry's leave the Wonderland for the Mirror Lakes spur — plank walkways over marshy meadow, then the end of maintained tread. The path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak. From there it is cross-country on the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak, between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to Point 6631 just north of the peak. Snowmelt water is often available here into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at about 6,300 ft is a common first night.

This is one of only two routes on Rainier that avoids significant glacier travel, which is its whole appeal; the cost is that it is long, loose and unfrequented, with about 12–13 miles and roughly 11,500 ft of gain to Point Success. Most parties take two days, often with a second camp dug into the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft.
runs: the southwest and west slopes of pyramid peak between roughly 6 000

text: A huge shield streaked with dikes like bolts of lightning is the proof, and you can see it from out on the glacier. This is the southernmost of the prominent subsummits on the ridge between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb, and it is identified by one feature rather than by its shape: the base of the tower carries an enormous shield of dark granite crisscrossed by hundreds of pale dikes running across it like bolts of lightning. That streaking is unmistakable and visible from well out on the glacier, so pick the tower off before you commit to a line across the ice. The climbing starts in a clean dihedral just left of the dike-streaked shield, roughly twenty feet above the snow, and the bergschrund or moat at the foot of it is the first thing to assess, because it decides whether that start is reachable at all on the day. If the wall in front of you is uniform dark granite with no lightning-streak dikes, you are beneath the wrong subsummit and should continue south along the base. Once on it, the first pitch tiptoes rightward across parallel dikes for about forty feet to the very edge of the face; that stretch takes essentially no protection and a fall on it is long, with cracks only appearing higher up.
runs: feet to the very edge of the face

This is the southernmost of the prominent subsummits on the ridge between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb, and it is identified by one feature rather than by its outline: the base of the tower carries an enormous shield of dark granite crisscrossed by hundreds of pale dikes running across it like bolts of lightning. That streaking is unmistakable and visible from well out on the glacier, so pick the tower off before committing to a line across the ice. Leave the glacier at the tower's foot. The climbing starts in a clean dihedral just left of the dike-streaked shield, roughly twenty feet above the snow, and the bergschrund or moat at the base is the first thing to assess, because it decides whether that start is reachable at all. If the wall in front of you is uniform dark granite with no lightning-streak dikes, you are beneath the wrong subsummit and should keep going south along the base. Once established, the first pitch tiptoes rightward across parallel dikes for about forty feet to the very edge of the face and takes essentially no gear for that whole stretch; cracks appear higher and the pitch runs the better part of a full rope length.

text: A series of corners, overhangs, and slabs to the top of Osprey Wall with excellent crystal pocket holds; protection is a mix of bolts and natural gear, with the third pitch fully bolted.
